changes.stem: Why do many airliners' wing tips turn upward?
options: They weaken the tip swirl, saving fuel

explanationWrong: Scraping the runway isn't the concern. Winglets are there to save fuel. Air spills round the wing tip from the higher pressure underside and spins off in a swirl that causes drag. NASA engineer Richard Whitcomb showed that an upturned tip weakens that swirl.

Crosswinds aren't the reason. At the wing tip, air curls up from the higher pressure underside and spins off in a swirl that causes drag. NASA engineer Richard Whitcomb showed that an upturned tip weakens the swirl, cutting drag and fuel use.

Winglets don't stiffen the wing. They help because of the swirl of air at the tip, which curls up from the higher pressure underside and causes drag. An upturned tip weakens that swirl, so the plane burns less fuel.

edits.note: Option D used to be partly true (NASA did note that longer wings wouldn't fit airport gates), so a wrong option can't be. It's replaced with one that's plainly wrong, with its own explanation.
